pamphlet_excerpts: Natural Foraging Versus Stabling: Although horses are built to forage, it is not always practical to put a horse out to pasture (p. 16).
Activity-Based Feeding Guidelines: When feeding, there are a few rules to follow. Provide an amount of feed appropriate to the horse's activity level (p. 16).
Risks of Overfeeding Horses: Too much feed can cause digestive and circulatory problems (p. 16).
Consequences of Underfeeding Rations: Too little feed can lead to a loss of energy, and it could harm the horse's overall condition (p. 16).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Prevent Excess Grain Intake: Too much feed can cause digestive and circulatory problems (p. 16).
Step 2 - Maintain Adequate Daily Rations: Too little feed can lead to a loss of energy, and it could harm the horse's overall condition (p. 16).
Step 3 - Provide Fresh Water Before Feed: If your horse is stabled, give it clean water before feeding. Do not feed a horse that is tired or overheated (p. 16).
Step 4 - Cool Horses Before Feeding: Let a horse cool off sufficiently after exercise or work before allowing it to eat. Water is critical for a horse's health (p. 16).

Susceptibility Across Horse Ages: Thoroughbreds 2 to 3 years old are the most commonly affected, but horses of any age can become afflicted (p. 48).
Ophthalmic Inflammation Warning Signs: Symptoms include redness, increased tearing, half-closed, and painful-looking eyes, as well as swelling and tenderness of the eye or eyes (p. 48).
Causes of Equine Azoturia: Though eating too much while idle is the cause, azoturia is regarded as a more complex issue, involving type of diet, vitamin deficiencies (p. 48).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Check Eyes for Tearing: Symptoms include redness, increased tearing, half-closed, and painful-looking eyes, as well as swelling and tenderness of the eye or eyes (p. 48).
Step 2 - Reduce Grain During Idle Days: Though eating too much while idle is the cause, azoturia is regarded as a more complex issue, involving type of diet, vitamin deficiencies (p. 48).
Step 3 - Watch for Hindquarter Muscle Cramping: When being worked or exercised again after the idleness, the loins and quarters stiffen and cramps result (p. 48).

quiz_item.question: What is the proper technique for asking a horse to back up four straight paces without causing resistance?
options: A. Stand up in the stirrups and pull steadily backward with all your strength on one rein.
B. Use light, rhythmic rein cues combined with leg support while never jerking on the horse's mouth.
C. Kick both heels vigorously while dropping the reins completely onto the horse's neck.
D. Lean forward over the pommel and tap the horse between the ears.

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Use light, rhythmic rein cues combined with leg support while never jerking on the horse's mouth.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Because horses naturally dislike moving backward and will brace against harsh pulling, a rider must never jerk on the mouth and instead use gentle, coordinated rein and leg cues (p. 49).

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Allowing a tired or overheated horse to eat before cooling down diverts blood flow and disrupts digestion, which can trigger colic or laminitis (p. 52).
